items.passage: Anna has a small dog called Pip. Every morning she takes him to the park before school. Pip likes to run after the birds.
items.prompt: When does Anna take Pip to the park?
options: In the morning
After school
At night
On Sundays
items.answer: In the morning

items.passage: The cafe on Green Street opens at eight o'clock. It sells coffee, tea and fresh bread. It is closed on Mondays.
items.prompt: Which day is the cafe closed?
options: Monday
Sunday
Saturday
Friday
items.answer: Monday

items.passage: Luis lives in a flat above a bookshop. His flat is small, but it has a big window. From the window he can see the river.
items.prompt: What can Luis see from his window?
options: The river
The bookshop
A garden
The mountains
items.answer: The river

items.passage: Sara goes to work by bus. The bus takes twenty minutes. When it rains, she takes a taxi instead.
items.prompt: How does Sara travel when it rains?
options: By taxi
By bus
By bike
On foot
items.answer: By taxi

items.passage: The library is next to the school. It has books, computers and a quiet room for studying. Children can borrow five books at a time.
items.prompt: How many books can children borrow?
options: Five
Two
Ten
Three
items.answer: Five

items.passage: Tom works from home three days a week. On Tuesdays and Thursdays he takes the train to the office, which takes about an hour each way. He does not mind the journey, because he uses the time to read.
items.prompt: What does Tom do on the train?
options: He reads
He sleeps
He works
He calls colleagues
items.answer: He reads

items.passage: Elena works in a small bakery near the station. She starts at five in the morning and bakes bread for the shops nearby. She does not mind the early start, because she finishes at lunchtime and has the whole afternoon free.
items.prompt: Why does Elena not mind starting work so early?
options: She finishes at lunchtime and has the afternoon free
The bakery is close to the station
She only works at the weekend
She bakes bread with her family
items.answer: She finishes at lunchtime and has the afternoon free

items.passage: The swimming pool is open every day except Wednesday. Tickets cost four euros, but students pay half price if they show a card. The pool is busiest after six in the evening.
items.prompt: How can a student pay less for a ticket?
options: By showing a student card
By coming after six
By buying several tickets
By swimming on Wednesday
items.answer: By showing a student card

items.passage: Marc wanted to cook a fish soup for his friends, so he went to the market after work. He arrived at six, but the fish stall had already packed up for the day. He bought vegetables instead and made a soup without fish.
items.prompt: What happened when Marc got to the market?
options: The fish stall had already closed
The market was too expensive
He forgot what he needed
He bought a ready-made soup
items.answer: The fish stall had already closed

items.passage: The camping site by the lake has thirty places for tents. Visitors must book in summer, because it fills up quickly. In spring and autumn it is usually possible to arrive without booking.
items.prompt: Why should visitors book in summer?
options: The site fills up quickly then
The site is closed in spring
Tents are more expensive then
There are only thirty visitors
items.answer: The site fills up quickly then

items.passage: When Martin first moved to Toronto, he found the city overwhelming. The pace was faster than anything he had known, and for months he kept to his own neighbourhood. Gradually that changed. He now says the variety of the place is the reason he stays.
items.prompt: How did Martin's view of Toronto change?
options: He found it overwhelming at first but now values its variety
He enjoyed it at first but now finds it too fast
He still finds it overwhelming but has made friends
He disliked the city and plans to leave
items.answer: He found it overwhelming at first but now values its variety

items.passage: The town council introduced a free bicycle scheme last spring. Anyone can take a bike from one of the racks and leave it at another. The scheme has been popular, though the council admits that repairs are costing more than it expected.
items.prompt: What problem does the council mention?
options: Repairs cost more than expected
Nobody uses the bicycles
There are too few racks
The bicycles are being stolen
items.answer: Repairs cost more than expected

items.passage: Rosa trained as an architect but left the profession after six years. She now restores old furniture in a workshop behind her house. She earns less than she did, but she says she has never regretted the change.
items.prompt: What does Rosa say about leaving architecture?
options: She does not regret it, despite earning less
She regrets it because she earns less
She plans to return to the profession
She left because the work was too hard
items.answer: She does not regret it, despite earning less

items.passage: The festival was due to take place in the main square, but heavy rain in the week before left the ground unusable. Organisers moved it to the sports hall at two days' notice. Attendance was lower than usual, which they blamed on the late change rather than the weather itself.
items.prompt: What do the organisers think caused the lower attendance?
options: The late change of venue
The rain on the day itself
The cost of the tickets
The size of the sports hall
items.answer: The late change of venue

items.passage: Most guidebooks send visitors to the cathedral and the old bridge, and both are worth an hour. But the part of the city that stays with people is usually the market district, which few guidebooks mention at all.
items.prompt: What does the writer suggest about the market district?
options: It is memorable but often left out of guidebooks
It is the main attraction in every guidebook
It is less interesting than the cathedral
It is difficult for visitors to reach
items.answer: It is memorable but often left out of guidebooks

items.passage: For decades the museum displayed its collection exactly as the founder had arranged it in 1912, on the grounds that the arrangement was itself a historical document. Critics argued that this reverence carried a cost: visitors were shown the taste of one Edwardian collector rather than the objects themselves. The trustees have now approved a partial rehang.
items.prompt: Why did critics object to the original arrangement?
options: It showed one collector's taste rather than the objects
It damaged the objects over time
It was too expensive to maintain
It had been changed too often since 1912
items.answer: It showed one collector's taste rather than the objects

items.passage: Public discussion tends to treat technological progress as self-evidently good, assuming that innovation improves society on its own. That assumption has a blind spot. Without oversight, new tools can just as easily entrench existing advantages, widen economic gaps and push already marginal groups further to the edge.
items.prompt: According to the passage, what can innovation do without oversight?
options: Entrench existing advantages and widen economic gaps
Improve society automatically
Remove the need for regulation
Reduce the influence of public discussion
items.answer: Entrench existing advantages and widen economic gaps

items.passage: Remote work was widely predicted to empty city centres. Four years on, the picture is more mixed. Offices are indeed quieter midweek, but the cafes, gyms and shops around them have not closed in the numbers forecast. What has changed is the rhythm: the centre is busy on three days and subdued on two.
items.prompt: What does the passage say has actually changed in city centres?
options: The weekly rhythm of activity, rather than the overall level
The number of businesses, which fell as predicted
The kinds of shops that trade there
Nothing measurable has changed
items.answer: The weekly rhythm of activity, rather than the overall level

items.passage: Despite the well-documented benefits of immunisation, a section of the public continues to believe that vaccines carry hidden risks. Public health officials note that it is rarely the science that fails to reach people. What sustains the doubt is the speed with which fear circulates compared with correction.
items.prompt: What do officials identify as the main obstacle?
options: Fear spreads faster than correction does
The scientific evidence is incomplete
Vaccines do carry hidden risks
People have not heard the scientific case
items.answer: Fear spreads faster than correction does

items.passage: The publisher had expected the memoir to sell modestly and printed accordingly. Then a single review, written by a critic with no particular following, was shared several hundred thousand times in a weekend. The second printing was ordered before the first had reached the shops.
items.prompt: What does the passage suggest about the book's success?
options: It came from an unexpected source rather than the critic's reputation
It was the result of careful planning by the publisher
It was caused by the critic's large following
It happened slowly over several months
items.answer: It came from an unexpected source rather than the critic's reputation

items.passage:
For much of the twentieth century, city planners treated parks as pleasant but optional additions, the first thing cut when budgets tightened. That attitude has quietly reversed. As cities have grown denser and summers hotter, green spaces have come to be seen less as decoration than as infrastructure, performing measurable work that concrete cannot.

None of this makes parks simple to provide. Land in crowded cities is expensive, and a space meant for everyone must be designed with unusual care, or it risks serving no one well. But the old question, whether a city can afford its parks, is increasingly giving way to a sharper one: whether it can afford to be without them.
items.prompt: What central change in thinking does the passage describe?
options: Parks are now seen as essential infrastructure rather than decoration
Cities have found parks cheap and easy to provide
Cities increasingly regard parks as too expensive to justify
Planners have stopped cutting park budgets entirely
items.answer: Parks are now seen as essential infrastructure rather than decoration

items.passage: While a good deal of research links education to societal development, we should be careful not to mistake correlation for causation. Societies evolve through a complex interplay of factors, of which education is undoubtedly an integral part, but not the sole driving force.
items.prompt: What does the author imply about studies linking education to development?
options: They show a real connection, but not that education alone causes development
They prove education drives development more than any other factor
Their findings are unreliable and should be set aside
They overlook the link between education and development
items.answer: They show a real connection, but not that education alone causes development

items.passage: The argument for open-plan offices rested on an intuition about collaboration: remove the walls and conversation will follow. The evidence has been unkind to it. When one large firm tracked interactions before and after a move, face-to-face exchange fell by roughly seventy per cent, while email and messaging rose to fill the gap. People, it seems, respond to the loss of privacy by withdrawing into channels they can control.
items.prompt: What does the evidence suggest about open-plan offices?
options: Removing walls reduced face-to-face contact rather than increasing it
Collaboration increased as the designers had predicted
Employees preferred the new layout to the old one
Email use fell once people could speak directly
items.answer: Removing walls reduced face-to-face contact rather than increasing it

items.passage: Restoration is never a neutral act. Every decision to return a building to a particular moment is also a decision to erase the centuries on either side of it. The nineteenth-century restorers who stripped medieval churches back to an imagined original were not preserving history so much as choosing which part of it deserved to survive.
items.prompt: What is the author's main point about restoration?
options: Choosing a period to restore to means erasing other periods
Medieval churches were restored more carefully than other buildings
Restoration should always return a building to its original state
Nineteenth-century restorers preserved history faithfully
items.answer: Choosing a period to restore to means erasing other periods

items.passage: Economists have long treated the minimum wage as a straightforward test case: raise the price of labour and employers will buy less of it. A generation of empirical work has complicated that expectation without quite overturning it. Modest increases appear to cost few jobs; large ones, in low-wage regions, are another matter. The disagreement now is less about direction than about where the threshold lies.
items.prompt: What is the current state of the disagreement?
options: It concerns the threshold at which increases cost jobs
It concerns whether raising wages costs any jobs at all
It has been settled by recent empirical work
It concerns whether employers respond to prices
items.answer: It concerns the threshold at which increases cost jobs

items.passage: It has become customary to describe the archive as a neutral repository, a place where the past is kept rather than made. The metaphor flatters everyone involved. In practice an archive is the residue of a long series of judgements about what merited keeping, made by people with no obligation to explain themselves and no expectation that anyone would later ask. The historian who treats the surviving record as a sample of the past, rather than as a selection from it, has mistaken the nature of the evidence before a single document is read.
items.prompt: What criticism does the author make of historians?
options: Treating the surviving record as representative rather than selected
Failing to read enough of the documents available to them
Relying on archives instead of other kinds of evidence
Refusing to accept that archives are neutral repositories
items.answer: Treating the surviving record as representative rather than selected

items.passage: The received account of the printing press credits it with the spread of literacy, and by extension with the Reformation, the scientific revolution and much else besides. The chronology sits awkwardly with the claim. Literacy rates in much of Europe moved little for a century after Gutenberg, and where they did rise, cheap paper and vernacular schooling track the change more closely than movable type. None of this makes the press unimportant. It does suggest that it was one condition among several, and that the habit of treating it as the cause owes more to the tidiness of the story than to the evidence.
items.prompt: What is the author's position on the printing press?
options: It was one contributing condition, not the single cause it is made out to be
It had no meaningful effect on literacy or later change
It caused the rise in literacy, as the received account holds
Its effects were confined to the century after Gutenberg
items.answer: It was one contributing condition, not the single cause it is made out to be

items.passage: Defenders of the reform present it as a technical adjustment, and in the narrow sense they are right: the change alters a formula, not a principle. Yet formulas are where principles are enacted, and a body that can revise the calculation without revisiting the commitment behind it has found a way to legislate while appearing merely to administer. The distinction between the two has always been thinner than constitutional theory allows.
items.prompt: What is the author's objection to the reform?
options: A technical change lets a body legislate under the appearance of administering
The formula in question was calculated incorrectly
Constitutional theory does not distinguish legislation from administration
The reform revisits a commitment that should have been left alone
items.answer: A technical change lets a body legislate under the appearance of administering

items.passage: Her early novels were praised for a restraint that later critics have read as evasion. The charge is not unfounded, though it assumes a writer owes her material a full accounting. What the restraint achieves, in the best of the books, is a kind of pressure: the reader supplies what the prose withholds, and is implicated in the supplying. Whether that is a technique or an alibi is a question the novels themselves seem content to leave open.
items.prompt: What does the author say about the restraint in the novels?
options: It makes the reader complete the meaning, and the books leave its status unresolved
It is clearly an evasion of the material, as later critics argue
It is a technique the novels explicitly defend
It was praised early on but has since been shown to be a flaw
items.answer: It makes the reader complete the meaning, and the books leave its status unresolved

items.passage: Proponents of prediction markets argue that they aggregate dispersed knowledge more honestly than polls, because participants stake something on being right. The mechanism is real, and where markets are liquid their record is respectable. The difficulty is that the questions most worth forecasting are precisely those on which few people will trade: distant, ambiguous in resolution, or morally charged enough that betting looks unseemly. The instrument works best on the questions we least need it for.
items.prompt: What limitation of prediction markets does the passage identify?
options: They function poorly on exactly the questions that matter most
Participants have no incentive to be accurate
Their record is worse than that of conventional polls
They resolve ambiguous questions too slowly
items.answer: They function poorly on exactly the questions that matter most
